newsitem.title: GERMANY: German recovery seen faltering before pickup.
newsitem.headline: German recovery seen faltering before pickup.

text.p: Germany's recovery may falter in the fourth quarter but will pick up in 1997, a key year when European Union members must earn their economic spurs to qualify for a planned single currency, analysts said on Wednesday.
Their prediction came against a backdrop of strong exports, firm dollar, stable prices and low interest rates -- and despite a mixed picture painted by the latest economic data.
Industry orders in October, reported on Wednesday, rose 2.9 percent month-on-month after a 3.4 percent fall in September.
Industrial output fell 1.8 percent in October after a drop of 0.6 percent, data showed on the previous day, perhaps linked to labour unrest over employer attempts to cut sick pay.
Analysts said fourth quarter gross domestic product (GDP) would struggle to add to growth of 0.8 percent in the third quarter, based on adjusted Bundesbank figures.
"It is clear that fourth quarter growth will be weaker," said economist Gerhard Grebe at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, who forecasts final quarter rise in GDP of 0.3 percent.

But with industry stocks low, a pickup in orders could soon feed through into output, Grebe said. He expected the economy to chug along with growth averaging 0.5-0.6 percent per quarter next year and full-year 1997 growth at around 2.3 percent.

That is just below the official government forecast of 2.5 percent. It is a critical figure since it underpins government spending plans intended to meet the Maastricht Treaty's deficit target for the country to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

"Overall...Germany is suffering from the loose money/tight fiscal stance which has been concocted by the central bank and the government in the run-up to EMU," HSBC economist Stephen King said in a note.
"The likely result is a soggy recovery with occasional significant interruptions." King's 1997 growth forecast is 2.4 percent after 1.3 percent this year.
Analysts said the Ifo economic institute's recent survey of business confidence in western Germany for October -- seen as a key leading indicator -- also pointed to rising output.
But they cautioned that although the German economy is picking up it is still too dependent on exports and lacks the support of internal demand to make recovery decisive.

"Despite the much-improved Ifo business index and the very strong third quarter GDP growth, the industrial indicators still raise doubts over the dynamics of this recovery," analysts at Trinkaus Capital Management wrote.
The flip-side to weak consumption is that price pressures remain low in a deflationary domestic environment. That could still leave the door open to an interest rate cut next year.
The Bundesbank's hawkish position on inflation has eased since a sharp autumn spike in oil prices barely registered on the retail price index, Grebe said.
That, he added, has given the central bank more scope to allow the mark to fall against the dollar, which should in turn further stoke Germany's exports.
"(Bundesbank President Hans) Tietmeyer has been saying he favoured a strong dollar at around 1.55 marks," Grebe said. "Now he says he is not opposed to a stronger dollar."
The mark jumped on forex markets early in the day on the GDP data, but fell back later to around 1.5635 to the dollar.
Analysts said a 3.2 percent recovery in third quarter investment pointed towards a broader recovery.

"We saw quite a big increase in capital spending. One thing we have been concerned about is that there hasn't been very much investment behind the recovery in the German economy," Rob Hayward at Bank of America in London commented.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said a sustained recovery in both investment and output would be needed to stimulate job creation in Germany.

Seasonally adjusted unemployment hit a post-unification high of 4.04 million in October. Analysts polled by Reuters said they expected to see a rise of between 15,000 and 45,000 in November unemployment, due out on Thursday.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-2609750
